chapter: Quill, Cannonball and finding a voice
title: Gene Quill stories and his decline
summary: Quill's humor, hearing him as a kid, 'You imitate Charlie Parker', and how he burned out.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: It’s kind of silly in jazz but that was Quill’s thing. Or, he’d be at a bar and there’d be a young guy drinking and uh Gene’d say, “Well, what are you killing yourself over?” [Both laugh] And I remember one time he played with the Johnny Richards band and he just played a blazing solo. I think it was on “Tappan Zee,”one of his featured tunes, faster than hell and he played a brilliant solo, Well I heard him play with Art Mooney’s band up in Springfield Massachusetts when I was a kid, he had a couple of years on me but
he was very young then. But he did uh I remember hearing, um, I was, I was starting to play the alto and he played a solo on “Stars and Stripes Forever,” like a jazz arrangement …

… and I said “Whoa.” So, I knew who he I sort of knew who he was but when we became tight. Anyway, he played this blazing solo, he could play fast, man, great clarinet player too. And uh as he came off the bandstand, somebody at the table right in, in the, at the table right near the Birdland bandstand as he went, went by to go back to the dressing room somebody said, “Gene Quill, all you’re doing is imitating Charlie Parker.” And he whipped around and he handed him his horn, and he said, “Here, you imitate Charlie Parker.”
Not so easy. That’s all you’re doing? Here, [chuckles] you want to try it?

Yeah, especially back then. Yeah. But he couldn’t handle success. He had uh, you know, he burned himself out, went back to Atlantic City and had a lot of health problems and didn’t quite make it. But I think of him a lot, we were brothers.
